title: Remaining import tariffs
summary: Many imported goods still attract a tariff, mostly at 5%, under the Customs Tariff Act 1995. The Government abolished almost 500 'nuisance' tariffs from 1 July 2024. The Productivity Commission estimates removing the remaining tariffs would add 0.13 to 0.25% to GDP.
direction_rationale: Tariffs raise the price of imported goods and inputs, shelter some domestic producers from competition and add customs compliance costs.

verified.notes: An existing setting: no commencement date is recorded. The 2024 abolition is from Treasury's consultation and press coverage of the announcement.

review.notes: Drafted by AI-assisted desk research on 28 October 2026 (phase 4 of the productivity framework pivot) from the sources cited. Not yet checked by a person: verify the description, industries and assessment before use.

assessment.summary: The tariffs left after decades of reform, mostly 5%. They raise prices for buyers of imported goods and inputs and add customs paperwork, for little protection.

marks.reason: Tariffs shelter domestic producers from import competition and raise input costs.
Importers must classify goods and prove origin to pay or avoid duty.

assessment.confidence_note: The Productivity Commission modelled removing all remaining tariffs at +0.13 to 0.25% of GDP.
